articles.title: Bridge Street in Heywood closed as emergency services attend incident
articles.excerpt: the source reports a closure on Bridge Street, with photographs showing a police cordon and a fire engine at the scene.
articles.content_html:
Bridge Street in Heywood has been closed by emergency services, according to a report shared by the source on Saturday evening, 24 October.

Photographs accompanying the broadcaster's Facebook post show police tape across the road, a marked police car blocking access and a fire engine at the scene.

The post does not explain the nature of the incident. It contains no confirmed information about injuries, the reason for the cordon or when the road will reopen.

The presence of firefighters does not, by itself, confirm that a fire has occurred.

Drivers approaching Bridge Street should allow extra time and follow any directions given by emergency services. The photographs show a closure, but the precise extent of the restrictions has not been established.

articles.title: Weather warning issued for Rochdale as Storm Boelo approaches
articles.excerpt: Residents in Rochdale are advised to prepare for potential disruption as Storm Boelo is expected to bring strong winds and heavy rain this weekend.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Rochdale are being warned to prepare for disruption as Storm Boelo approaches the borough this afternoon. The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for wind, predicting strong gusts that could cause damage to buildings and trees, as well as affecting local rivers and roads.

Forecasters expect Storm Boelo to bring a very windy and wet spell this weekend, with strong winds spreading across northern parts of the UK on Saturday afternoon. Gusts of 55-65 mph are likely widely, with some coastal and exposed areas potentially experiencing gusts of 70-80 mph or more, particularly in Scotland and the far north of England.

The storm follows closely on the heels of Storm Austen, which recently impacted the south, south-west, and parts of Wales, with winds reaching up to 84 mph. Residents are encouraged to stay updated on weather conditions and take necessary precautions to ensure their safety during the storm's passage.

As Storm Boelo is expected to persist overnight and through much of Sunday, it is crucial for local residents to remain vigilant and prepared for possible disruptions. This weather event highlights the importance of being aware of severe weather warnings and taking proactive measures to protect homes and property.

articles.title: Regeneration scheme near Rochdale station progresses with new homes
articles.excerpt: A regeneration project around Rochdale station is advancing, with 81 homes under construction and plans for 33 new apartments, enhancing connectivity to the town centre.
articles.content_html:
A significant regeneration scheme around Rochdale station is making notable progress, with 81 homes currently under construction adjacent to Rochdale’s Central Retail Park. This development is part of a broader initiative aimed at improving connectivity between the train station and the town centre, which has historically been a purposeful distance apart.

In addition to the homes being built, plans are underway for 33 new apartments on a brownfield site located at the junction of Maclure Road and Station Road. This project is particularly significant as it will feature the first affordable net zero homes in the housing scheme, aligning with modern sustainability goals.

The regeneration project, which received approval several years ago, has secured £15 million in funding. Local authorities faced challenges in attracting investment for the project until last year, but the current construction is already benefiting the local economy and community. John Rennie Place, a key component of the scheme, is scheduled for completion in December 2027.

This development not only aims to enhance the residential landscape of Rochdale but also seeks to transform the area around the station, which has shifted from a focus on transporting goods to serving passengers. As the project progresses, it is expected to contribute positively to the local community and economy.

Some 81 two, three-and four-bedroom homes are currently under construction on vacant land next to Rochdale’s Central Retail Park. This forms part of a wider scheme to create a connection between the train station and the town centre. The wider regeneration of the area around Rochdale railway station also involves the creation of a new public square in front of the station and 33 new apartments on a brownfield site on the corner of Maclure Road and Station Road. The train station in Rochdale was once a hub for industrial business generations ago, so the distance between the station and the town centre was purposeful separation. But as times changed, society changed and the station suddenly started transporting people, not goods. This is why there is an idea to improve access and avenues from the station and the main hub of the town. This 81-home development, known as John Rennie Place, in honour of the late Scottish Civil engineer who masterminded the Rochdale Canal, got under way in November last year, and is due for completion in December 2027. The project, approved years ago, was unlocked following a successful bid for £15m from the government’s Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund. The transformation has been on the cards for a long time, but the local authority struggled to get the investment until last year. The properties will be the first affordable net zero homes delivered as part of a housing scheme supported by the council. The local authority says the development is already delivering benefits to the local economy and community. Contractor Willmott Dixon, working on behalf of the council, has already spent £3.3m with local civil engineering firm, Hovington Ltd, and supported a total of 95 weeks of apprenticeship and T-Level training, including three T-Level placements from Hopwood Hall College. Seven local people are also employed on the project, including two people who were previously unemployed, with the council’s work and skills team supporting the recruitment. Tommy Patterson, 22, from Middleton, is one of the local people working on the new homes. He said: “I had been out of work for six months when the job centre arranged for me to get my CSCS card and that led to me securing a scaffolding apprenticeship here on site. I have always worked and had been let go, so getting this job was a lifeline. “I live on my own and I was struggling to pay my bills. It’s great to work here. Everyone is lovely; it’s a smashing team.” Daniel Fletcher, 17, is studying for a T Level in design, surveying and planning at Hopwood Hall College, said: “I really like it here. I’ve been talking to the different trades delivering this project, so I’ve been exposed to different parts of the job, and I have the freedom to go onto site on my own. It’s already changed massively since I started in the summer.” The project is being led by Rochdale Development Agency (RDA) on behalf of Rochdale Borough Council. Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for housing and regeneration at Rochdale Borough Council, said: ”We want local people and businesses to feel the benefit of local projects and it’s great to see that these benefits are already being felt on this development before a single house has even been completed. “By ensuring that social value is embedded in our procurement system, we’re making sure that local people are invested in the extensive regeneration which is taking place on their doorstep and are benefitting from the economic transformation we’re spearheading across the borough. That’s how it should be and how it will continue to be.” Work to create 142 apartments next to the new homes is ongoing, with the procurement of a delivery partner expected to get underway soon. articles.title: Community efforts revive historic Lodge Mill after devastating fire
articles.excerpt: Lodge Mill in Middleton, a historic site dating back to 1850, is seeing a revival thanks to community support following a fire that left it in ruins.
articles.content_html:
Lodge Mill, one of the oldest mills in Middleton, is undergoing a revival after a devastating fire left the historic structure nearly destroyed. The fire, which occurred earlier this year, resulted in the loss of significant parts of the mill, including a children's dance studio and an ice cream parlour. Fortunately, no injuries were reported during the incident.

The mill, which dates back to around 1850, was deemed uninsurable following the fire, complicating efforts for its restoration. However, local residents and volunteers have rallied together to support the rebuilding efforts. A GoFundMe page was established, raising over £7,000 to aid in the restoration process, demonstrating the community's commitment to preserving this historic landmark.

Martin and Paula, who were actively working on renovating the three floors above Lodge Mill prior to the fire, are now at the forefront of the recovery efforts. Thanks to the dedication of volunteers, life is returning to Lodge Mill, with plans to restore it to its former glory.

The revival of Lodge Mill is significant not only for its historical value but also for the community spirit it embodies. As restoration efforts continue, the mill is set to become a focal point for local activities once again, highlighting the importance of community involvement in preserving local heritage.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The potential return of Lodge Mill | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The potential return of Lodge Mill George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 24, 2026 | 2 hours ago Print Community effort to clear up rubble at Lodge Mill in Middleton Lodge Mill in Middleton was devastated by a fire six months ago. Now there is hope for its future thanks to some dedicated business owners, volunteers and one avid ice cream fan. In March, firefighters were called to the massive blaze that left businesses in tatters and left the historic mill a shell. Several businesses were based on the ground floor of the building, believed to be one of the oldest mills in Middleton. A children’s dance studio, an ice cream parlour, a tea room, a dog chiropractor business and the Engine House event space, which held weddings, functions and parties, were all lost in the fire. The former silk and cotton mill, on Townley Street, dates back to around 1850. It was bought by couple Martin Cove and Paula Hickey in 2019, who were working passionately to renovate the three floors above. The pair have since kickstarted a fundraising campaign to restore the building soon after the fire, because the mill was uninsurable. Martin and Paula said the blaze ’caused the almost total loss of the main mill structure’. “No one was injured, and for that we are incredibly thankful,” the couple said at the time of the fire. “But we are heartbroken at the loss of not only our beloved Lodge Mill, but also the homes of the many local businesses and the community space we had all built together. “The outpouring of love and compassion from the people of Middleton and the surrounding area has given us the strength to carry on.” The GoFundMe page has raised just over £7,000 since it was launched six months ago. Thanks to a group of keen volunteers, life has returned to the mill. Rubble has been moved from the old Engine Room and more than 120 pallets of full bricks, Yorkshire Stone and specialty bricks have been picked up by hand and stacked. The annual duck race was held at the site in May, the ice cream shop has reopened and there are upcoming events for Halloween and Christmas. There is a long-term vision to bring the mill back into proper use again, with businesses on the ground floor and new flats above. But before that can happen, the site needs to be cleared. One keen volunteer is Dawn Alker, she visited The Ice Cream Shop at Lodge around eight years ago. She has returned many times since, but most recently as a volunteer. She said: “I went there for ice cream about seven or eight years ago and fell in love with the place. When it burnt down they asked for volunteers to clean it up. “Everyone goes down and chips in and does what they can on the day. “I used to be a manager in the NHS and now I am making a monster for Halloween in a burnt down mill. “It’s really nice to be working collectively. It’s turned into a community support project in a way. “I have mental health issues and I had stopped going outside and stayed inside too much. I started helping, selfishly, because I wanted the ice cream place back open again. “My mental health started to improve as I got moving more and others have said the same. “In terms of the project we have got to clear the site because it was bulldozed. Then the end goal is to rebuild it. “Then we want small businesses with flats over the top of them. That is just a vision at the moment. “It is going to  be a long project but it is going to be brilliant.” Dawn went on to say that the managers of Lodge Mill, Martin and Paula, have already instructed architects and looked at the structural integrity of the remaining walls at the mill. The business owners are hoping to submit planning proposals to the council in the coming months. articles.title: Rochdale housing development delayed again due to flooding concerns
articles.excerpt: The planning committee has deferred a decision on a housing scheme in Bamford, citing insufficient drainage details and historical flooding issues.
articles.content_html:
The Rochdale planning committee has once again delayed a decision on a proposed housing development in Bamford, which aims to build 45 homes as part of a larger 450-home project. The committee's latest meeting on October 22 revealed ongoing concerns about drainage and flooding on the site, which is located behind Greenvale.

In August, the committee had previously deferred the application from Wain Homes, expressing the need for more detailed plans to address historic drainage issues. Councillors noted that without a comprehensive masterplan for the entire development, they could not make an informed decision. The site, which was removed from green belt status under the Greater Manchester housing strategy, has been flagged for its seasonal flooding problems.

Objector Lisa Bailey highlighted the site's history of flooding, stating that the area is 'seasonally wet ground'. She urged the committee to ensure that infrastructure and access issues are adequately addressed before any development proceeds. Coun Stephen Anstee remarked on the unusually high number of conditions attached to the application, indicating that the proposal is not yet ready for approval.

Wain Homes' planning agent, Stephen Harris, argued that a flood risk management assessment was included in their application and that the other developers involved in the wider scheme had no objections. However, the committee decided to defer the application again, requesting a full report on drainage management from Wain Homes before proceeding.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council awards £1.1 million contract for young people's accommodation
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract worth over £1 million to Stepping Stone Projects for a new supported accommodation service for young people at risk of homelessness.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract valued at £1,108,081 to Stepping Stone Projects for the Rochdale Team Around the Young Person Accommodation Model (TAYPAS). This initiative aims to provide supported accommodation for young people aged 18 to 25 who are at risk of or experiencing homelessness. The contract will run from November 2, 2026, to November 1, 2029.

The TAYPAS model will deliver specialist, psychologically informed support within a newly developed, purpose-built facility that will feature 28 self-contained units. The service will offer 24/7 support and management, ensuring that young residents receive the assistance they need to transition into independent living.

This development is significant for the local community as it addresses the pressing issue of youth homelessness in Rochdale. By providing a safe and supportive environment, the council aims to improve the life chances of vulnerable young people in the area, helping them to build skills and confidence.

The next steps involve the construction and operational setup of the accommodation, which is expected to be completed in the coming months. This initiative not only reflects the council's commitment to supporting young people but also highlights the importance of addressing homelessness in the borough.

articles.title: £150 off energy bills: Rochdale households urged to watch for important letter
articles.excerpt: Warm Home Discount confirmation letters are arriving for eligible households, with the £150 energy credit applied over the winter rather than paid to everyone at once.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale residents who qualify for £150 off their energy bills are being urged to check their post as Warm Home Discount confirmation letters begin arriving.

The government started issuing letters on Thursday, 22 October, with correspondence continuing through to January 2027.

Around six million households across Britain are expected to benefit this winter. The letters will explain whether the discount will be applied automatically or whether the recipient needs to provide more information.

Anyone whose letter asks them to contact the Warm Home Discount helpline must do so before 26 February 2027.

The Warm Home Discount supports eligible households, including people receiving qualifying means tested benefits. Eligibility depends on the scheme’s rules, including benefit entitlement and the electricity account arrangements on the qualifying date.

For this winter, the qualifying date was 23 August 2026.

The £150 is normally applied directly to an eligible household’s electricity account. It is not a cash payment into a bank account, and there is no single payment day for everyone in Rochdale.

Eligible customers should receive their discount by 31 March 2027. Residents can check their supplier’s app, online account or bill for the credit.

The scheme is separate from the Winter Fuel Payment and Cold Weather Payments. Receiving the Warm Home Discount does not affect either entitlement.

For households watching every pound, the important step is to read the letter carefully and respond if action is requested.

Have you received your letter or seen the £150 appear on your energy account? Tell us your supplier and experience in the comments, keeping account numbers and personal details private.

articles.title: Does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall?
articles.excerpt: The house on Clegg Hall Road is real and well documented; the boggart belongs to Lancashire folklore, not to the record office.
articles.summary: The house on Clegg Hall Road is real and well documented; the boggart belongs to Lancashire folklore, not to the record office.
articles.body:
Short answer up front: the house, its date and fabric are documented; the murder tale and the angry spirit are part of oral and printed folklore rather than verified history.

Clegg Hall stands where the lane named for it climbs from the Roch to Smithy Bridge. Historic England lists the building as Grade II* (List Entry Number 1309615), dated to about 1610 and probably built for Theophilus Ashton; the list entry gives the grid reference SD9224214490 and a full architectural description of the porch, mullioned windows and interior features. These are matters of record you can look up on the National Heritage List for England. (Historic England's entry is the clearest, contemporary source for the building itself.)

The boggart story that brings visitors and late walkers to peer at the windows is older in print than the present stone house. Nineteenth century folklorists recorded a dramatic tradition: a grasping uncle, two orphan children disposed of so that the estate could be seized, and the afterwards-haunting of the place by a “Clegg Hall Boggart.” John Roby published a version in his Traditions of Lancashire; local writers and collectors repeated variants and an associated ballad. These accounts are the primary sources for the tale as a piece of Lancashire folk narrative.

Local historians have been explicit about the difference between the two kinds of source. The 1889 History of the Parish of Rochdale (Butterworth) notes the same tradition but warns that Roby’s retelling is “pure imagination” and that, although a ghost tradition was current in living memory and even gave rise to the local proverb “As ill as Clegg Hall boggart,” the violent episode is not supported by contemporary legal or manorial records cited in the book. In short, the building and its succession of owners are documented; the murderous episode lives in oral tradition and Victorian collectors' pages.

What the archives do show is a traceable ownership and building history. Butterworth’s parish history and the Victoria County History note the medieval family names associated with the site, the sale of the “capital messuage of Clegg called Clegg Hall” in the early 17th century, and the present house’s likely early-17th-century date. Historic England cites those county histories in its list entry for the architectural description. Those documentary strands are evidence of place and people; they do not, however, supply a contemporaneous 13th- or 14th-century record proving the murders described in the boggart legend.

That distinction matters because Victorian and earlier collectors often shaped and embellished what they heard. Folklore collectors were not court clerks; they recorded stories people told, sometimes smoothing gaps with imaginative detail. The Clegg Hall boggart is one of several regional boggarts recorded in Lancashire folklore, a useful example of how local names and proverbs can preserve a tale even when the archival trail is thin.

So does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall? If you mean “is there an archival, contemporaneous record that the alleged murders took place and left restless spirits?” the answer is no: researchers citing the local histories and the National Heritage List find no surviving medieval court roll or inquest that corroborates the dramatic crime as a documented fact. If you mean “is the boggart alive as a story?” the answer is yes: the spirit survives in printed folklore, in local sayings and in the imagination of visitors and readers.

If you want to follow the trail yourself, two good starting points are the Historic England listing for the house (for verified architectural and legal status) and the nineteenth century sources that collected the tale, notably John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and Butterworth’s History of the Parish of Rochdale, which explicitly separates the tradition from the documentary record. Those sources show where the story comes from and where the solid evidence begins and ends; beyond that the rest belongs to local legend and its afterlife in print and conversation.

articles.title: Rochdale projects £10.6 million spending on roads as repair programme targets borough streets
articles.excerpt: Council figures project £10.63 million in carriageway maintenance spending for 2026/27, around 26 per cent more than the previous year.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council projects spending £10.63 million on carriageway maintenance this financial year, around £2.16 million more than the previous year.

The figures appear in the council’s Highways Maintenance Transparency Report, which sets out how it maintains the borough’s roads and where the money goes.

Projected carriageway spending for 2026/27 is approximately 26 per cent higher than the £8.47 million recorded for 2025/26. The total includes £1.357 million in Department for Transport incentive funding.

The £10.63 million covers carriageway maintenance across the borough, including wider repairs and resurfacing. It is a spending projection for the full financial year, rather than a sum already spent.

The council’s capital programme lists 6.01 kilometres of road resurfacing and a further 7.10 kilometres of preventative treatment.

Named resurfacing locations include Whitegates Road in Middleton, Wordsworth Way and Seymour Street in Heywood, Belfield Lane, Kiln Lane and sections of Edenfield Road.

The report also records 10,998 permanent repairs and 364 temporary repairs during 2025/26, illustrating the scale of ongoing maintenance. Those figures count repairs rather than individual streets.

For residents, the practical question is what improvement that spending will deliver on the roads they use every day.

Which street should be a priority, and have previous repairs lasted? Tell us the road name and nearest junction in the comments so we can investigate specific locations.

articles.title: Roadworks on Elizabethan Way in Milnrow to begin on 23 October 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks will commence on Elizabethan Way in Milnrow from 9pm on Friday, 23 October 2026, until 6am on Saturday, 24 October 2026, or until the work is completed, whichever is sooner.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks will commence on Elizabethan Way in Milnrow from 9pm on Friday, 23 October 2026, until 6am on Saturday, 24 October 2026, or until the work is completed, whichever is sooner.

The roadworks will result in the temporary closure of part of Elizabethan Way, specifically between the roundabout junction and Newhey Road, covering a distance of approximately 418 metres. This closure will affect traffic in both directions, impacting local drivers and residents.

In addition to Elizabethan Way, nearby roads including Bridge Street, Dale Street, and Newhey Road may also experience disruptions during this period. Local residents and commuters are advised to plan their journeys accordingly and seek alternative routes where possible.

For further information and updates on the roadworks, residents can visit the Rochdale Borough Council website, where a map of the affected area is available.

articles.title: Rochdale Council seeks feedback on adult social care fee setting process
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council is inviting providers to participate in a survey aimed at improving the fee setting process for adult social care services.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has launched a survey to gather feedback from providers regarding its fee setting approach for adult social care commissioned services. This initiative aims to enhance transparency, engagement, and communication in the fee consultation process, ensuring it reflects the challenges faced by the provider market.

The council is particularly interested in understanding providers' experiences and identifying opportunities for improvement. The insights gained from this survey will inform future approaches to the fee setting process, which is crucial for maintaining high-quality and sustainable services for residents in Rochdale.

This consultation is part of the council's ongoing efforts to work collaboratively with service providers, valuing their expertise and input. Providers are encouraged to share their honest feedback, which will play a significant role in shaping the future of adult social care services in the borough.

The survey is available on the Rochdale Borough Council Consultation Hub and is open for participation now. Providers interested in contributing their views can access the survey at Rochdale Borough Council Consultation Hub. This engagement is vital as it directly impacts the quality and sustainability of care services available to the community.

articles.title: Your Trust hosts family activities during October half term in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Your Trust is offering a variety of family-friendly activities across multiple venues in Rochdale this October half term, including a special Halloween pool party.
articles.content_html:
Your Trust is set to host a range of activities for children and their families during the October half term, providing entertainment options across various venues in Rochdale. This initiative aims to keep families engaged and active during the school break, offering a mix of fun and festive events.

articles.title: From six modems to 580 staff: Rochdale’s Zen Internet puts people and planet alongside profit
articles.excerpt: Rochdale’s Zen Internet grew from £5,000 and six dial-up modems into a national broadband provider. Its B Corp approach puts customers, staff and the environment alongside profit.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale broadband business that began with £5,000 and six dial-up modems is highlighting how its B Corp approach shapes decisions about customers, staff and the environment.

Zen Internet was founded in 1995 after a conversation over a couple of pints between brothers Richard and Daniel Tang. Today, the company employs 580 people and supplies connectivity to homes and businesses across the UK.

Alongside that growth, Zen has retained its independence. Founder and chief executive Richard Tang remains its sole shareholder and has pledged never to sell the company.

What does being a B Corp mean?

Zen became a Certified B Corporation in 2020, joining a movement of businesses assessed against B Lab’s standards of social and environmental performance, transparency and accountability.

For Zen, that means considering the impact of its decisions on employees, customers, communities and the environment alongside financial performance.

The company points to practical examples, including two paid volunteering days each year for every employee, a fully UK based customer service team and a Contract Price Promise offering no mid-contract price rises.

Its community support includes donations to charities chosen through staff votes, involvement in the Rochdale Ambassadors scheme to attract investment and support for Rochdale Circle, which helps older residents live independently.

Zen also says it reinvests profits in its network and services, uses 100% renewable energy and refurbishes routers to extend their working lives and reduce waste.

One sourcing decision involved choosing an alternative to planned solar panels after identifying modern slavery concerns in the supply chain, despite the additional cost.

A business built for the long term

Tang says the company’s independence gives it freedom to make decisions with lasting benefits.

“From the moment I started Zen, I wanted to build a company that made a positive difference to the wider world, not just the bottom line,” he said.

“Becoming a B Corp was a natural fit given our freedom to make long-term choices, like keeping our support team in the UK and never raising prices mid-contract, that a purely shareholder-first business might struggle to justify.”

For Rochdale, Zen’s story is also one of a locally founded company growing into a national provider while continuing to employ hundreds of people.

For customers, the practical questions are straightforward: how much will a service cost over the full contract, who will answer when something goes wrong, and what happens to equipment when it is replaced?

Zen’s approach puts those everyday concerns at the centre of its business story.

What matters most when you choose a broadband provider: price, reliability, customer service or its wider impact? Share your thoughts in the comments.

articles.title: The Healey Dell prophecy: Eleanor Byron, Mother Bagden and what the records actually show
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the strange local tale that a Lady Eleanor was “maid, wife and widow in one day” — what early collectors wrote, what the Heritage Centre tells visitors, and what survives as documentary fact.
articles.summary: A short guide to the strange local tale that a Lady Eleanor was “maid, wife and widow in one day” — what early collectors wrote, what the Heritage Centre tells visitors, and what survives as documentary fact.
articles.body:
Healey Dell’s narrow gorge — the Thrutch — is one of Rochdale borough’s most durable story‑places. The best‑known version of the tale says a local noblewoman, usually called Lady Eleanor (later linked by tellings to the Byron family), visited a fortune‑teller named Mother Bagden; the woman predicted Eleanor would be a maid, a wife and a widow all in one day, and on her wedding night the bridegroom was killed. That dramatic sequence appears in the earliest printed collections of Lancashire lore and in the Dell’s modern visitor material, but the story’s status changes sharply once you separate nineteenth‑century collectors from contemporary medieval records. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

The oldest printed witness we can point to is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire, a book of collected oral tales published in the early 1800s; Roby preserves a long, romance‑style narrative set at Healey that includes a miller, a ‘Fairies’ Chapel’, a talisman and the fatal wedding night that fulfils the prophecy. Roby’s purpose was to record local storytelling rather than to provide documentary proof of medieval events, and his account reads as literary folklore rather than archival history. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Local antiquarians and guidebooks of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries amplified Roby’s version. The Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s trail guides and a short history leaflet reproduce the same outline: Ralph the miller, a messenger, Mother Bagden who claims intimate contact with a Fairy Queen, and the prediction that Eleanor will be “maid, wife and widow” in one day, followed by the death of her groom in a family feud. Those local guides attribute their narrative to older local histories such as William Robertson’s writings. The Heritage Centre presents the material as local myth and interpretation, alongside explanations of the Dell’s geology and industrial archaeology. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

What is demonstrably factual? Healey Dell is a managed nature reserve and visitor attraction at 121 Dell Road, with industrial archaeology (old mill sites, lodges) and a prominent Victorian railway viaduct that now forms part of a riverside trail. The viaduct is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. Those physical and administrative facts are public and documentable. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

What is folklore and what is missing from the archive? The supernatural elements — a Fairy Queen with prophetic power, spells that cause a bridegroom’s death, a named medieval Lady Eleanor whose wedding‑night fate is attested in contemporary court rolls or parish registers — lack contemporary documentary support. The story’s appearance in sources begins with nineteenth‑century collectors (Roby) and later local antiquarians (for example William Robertson as cited in modern guides); no contemporaneous medieval legal documents or parish entries confirming the prophecy or the precise characters named in the tale have been produced in those printed sources. In short: the prophecy belongs to the region’s oral and printed folklore tradition rather than to verified medieval record. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Why the story endures is straightforward: Healey Dell’s dramatic rock cleft, the Thrutch, looks for stories. A recess by the river invites the idea of a “Fairies’ Chapel”, and the valley’s history of mills, local rival families and visible ruins supplied the narrative scaffolding that collectors and guidebook writers later filled with characters and prophecy. The Heritage Centre explicitly treats the tale as part of the Dell’s storytelling — useful to visitors but not presented as archival fact. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

If you want to follow the trace yourself: read Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the early printed narrative; consult the Healey Dell Heritage Centre material for the local retelling and references to later antiquarians; and visit the Dell to see the viaduct, the Thrutch and the mill remains that inspired the story. If you hope to find a medieval legal record proving the prophecy, those proving documents are not cited in the early printed collectors and have not been produced in the local guides that preserve the tale — which is why historians and the Heritage Centre treat it as legend, however rooted in local memory it may be. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

articles.title: Rochdale wins gold at Britain in Bloom awards 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale town centre has been awarded gold in the 2026 Britain in Bloom awards, showcasing the borough's commitment to horticulture and community efforts.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale town centre has been awarded gold in the 2026 Britain in Bloom awards, triumphing in the Town and City Centres category. This recognition highlights the borough's dedication to horticulture and environmental responsibility, with Rochdale finishing ahead of competitors such as Floral Godalming, Shaftesbury in Bloom, and Sidcup Partners Ltd.

The judges praised the impressive floral displays contributed by Bowlee Garden Nursery, which played a significant role in Rochdale's successful entry. The town's submission included notable features such as the restored Grade I listed Town Hall, which received support from the National Lottery Heritage Fund, and the Baillie Street Quarter, both of which reflect the borough's commitment to regeneration and community spirit.

Rochdale's victory continues the borough's success in the Britain in Bloom competition, following Middleton's win in the previous year. The town has a history of excelling in these awards, and this latest achievement underscores the collective efforts of volunteers, local businesses, and council teams who contributed to the beautification of the area.

Councillor Tricia Ayrton, deputy leader of Rochdale Borough Council, expressed gratitude to all involved in the project. The win not only celebrates the hard work of the community but also aims to inspire further efforts in enhancing the local environment. With 44 finalists competing this year, Rochdale's gold award is a testament to what can be achieved through community collaboration.
